chapters.title: Suta's Arrival at Naimisharanya
paragraphs: In the sacred forest of Naimisharanya, under the leadership of the sage Shaunaka, many rishis had gathered for a long sacrificial session. At that time, the bard Suta Ugrashrava, who had already heard the story of the Mahabharata from Vyasa's disciple Vaishampayana, arrived humbly at this holy assembly.

The sages welcomed him warmly and asked him to share new, enlightening tales. Suta told them, with due humility, that he had been present at King Janamejaya's serpent sacrifice, where he had heard the vast, wondrous story composed by Maharishi Vedavyasa himself — the tale of the kings of the Bharata dynasty, of the great war between dharma and adharma, known as the Mahabharata.

Shaunaka and the whole assembly grew intensely eager, and they earnestly requested Suta to narrate this entire story from the beginning, in full detail, for this tale not only describes the glory and valor of kings but also reveals the subtlest secrets of dharma.

Suta, pleased by the sages' reverent curiosity, resolved to narrate the vast saga of the Mahabharata from its very beginning, reminding them that this story belongs not to a single royal line alone, but stands as a timeless mirror showing all of humanity the path of dharma, duty, and truth.
chapters.moral: A story that reveals the subtlest secrets of dharma becomes not mere history, but a living guide for every age.

chapters.title: Maharishi Vedavyasa and Lord Ganesha Compose the Epic
paragraphs: Suta went on to relate that when Maharishi Vedavyasa had, through his divine vision, composed this vast story filled with countless events entirely within his mind, he needed a scribe capable of keeping pace with the flow of his words.

He called upon Brahma, who advised him to pray to Lord Ganesha himself for this task. Vyasa invoked Ganesha, who agreed to the request but set one condition — that Vyasa must recite the verses continuously, without pause, or else he would abandon the work partway through.

Vyasa, in turn, set a clever counter-condition — that Ganesha would not write down any verse without first understanding its meaning. Thus, whenever Vyasa needed a brief pause to compose some complex, profound verse, he would recite one whose meaning would take Ganesha himself some time to grasp — and so both conditions were beautifully honored throughout.

Through this wondrous, divine collaboration, the vast text of the Mahabharata was composed, containing more than a hundred thousand verses. Vyasa himself named it "Jaya" (Victory), declaring that whoever hears or reads this story with a true heart becomes fit to achieve victory in every struggle of life.
chapters.moral: Even the greatest works are accomplished only through mutual respect and wise accommodation, however great the creators may be.

chapters.title: King Shantanu's Marriage to Ganga
paragraphs: The story truly begins with King Shantanu of Hastinapur, a righteous and just ruler of the Kuru dynasty. One day, wandering along the banks of the river Ganga, he saw a woman of extraordinary beauty — who was in truth the goddess Ganga herself, having taken human form.

Shantanu, enchanted by her matchless beauty, proposed marriage. Ganga accepted, but on one harsh condition — that the king would never question anything she did, however strange or painful it might seem, or else she would leave him at once, forever.

Shantanu, deep in the grip of his love, accepted this condition without pausing to think of what might follow. After their marriage, when Ganga bore seven sons one after another and cast each newborn into the river the moment he was born, Shantanu, bound by his vow, endured this agony in silence, unable to understand why his wife would commit such a cruel act.

When the time came for the birth of the eighth son, Shantanu's patience finally broke, and he stopped Ganga and demanded to know the reason for her acts — fully aware that this might end their marriage forever.
chapters.moral: A vow taken without deep reflection can bring the heart unbearable pain — yet the courage to learn the truth is never wasted.

chapters.title: The Birth of Devavrata and Ganga's Departure
paragraphs: Ganga revealed to Shantanu the hidden truth — that the seven sons were, in fact, seven of the eight Vasus, who had been cursed by a sage to be born in human form, and that Ganga had been freeing them from that curse the moment they were born, as swiftly as possible. This was an act of compassion, not cruelty.

But the eighth Vasu, named Dyau, had been cursed to live a long human life, and so Ganga had resolved to let this son live. She declared that, having now broken her condition, she would leave the king — but that she would take this son with her, raise and educate him properly, and return him to the king at the right time.

Years later, Ganga reappeared before Shantanu, bringing with her a radiant, extraordinarily accomplished young man. This boy was known as Devavrata, who had received complete instruction in all the scriptures, the art of weaponry, and statecraft from Maharishi Vasishtha, Parashurama, and Brihaspati himself.

Shantanu, overjoyed at receiving this extraordinary, virtuous son, proclaimed Devavrata the crown prince of Hastinapur, knowing that his kingdom was now secure in the hands of an heir exceptionally accomplished in dharma, valor, and knowledge alike.
chapters.moral: What seems like a curse or an affliction is sometimes only the cloak of deep compassion — its true meaning is revealed only in time.

chapters.title: Satyavati and Bhishma's Terrible Vow
paragraphs: Some years later, Shantanu fell deeply in love with Satyavati, a fisherman's daughter whose body carried a divine fragrance. But Satyavati's father set a harsh condition for the marriage — that only Satyavati's own offspring should be declared the future king of Hastinapur, not Devavrata.

Shantanu, hearing this condition, fell into a moral dilemma — he wished neither to deny his eldest, worthy son Devavrata his rightful place, nor could he give up his love for Satyavati. And so he sank into a deep sorrow, without revealing his inner anguish to anyone.

Devavrata, learning the reason for his father's uncharacteristic melancholy, went himself to the fisherman-king and declared that he was renouncing his own claim to the throne forever, so that his father could marry Satyavati.

The fisherman-king raised one further concern — that in the future, Devavrata's own children might challenge this renunciation. At this, Devavrata took the terrible, unprecedented vow that earned him the name "Bhishma" (the Formidable) — that he would remain unmarried his whole life, never desire the throne, and, living in complete celibacy, would always faithfully protect the throne of Hastinapur, whoever might sit upon it. The gods showered flowers from the heavens in honor of this extraordinary vow.
chapters.moral: Giving up one's own entire right and happiness for a father's contentment is the supreme example of true filial duty and selfless sacrifice.

chapters.title: Vichitravirya's Marriage and Untimely Death
paragraphs: Shantanu and Satyavati had two sons, Chitrangada and Vichitravirya. Chitrangada died an untimely death in battle against a Gandharva, and so Vichitravirya became king of Hastinapur while still a child, though the actual reins of government remained in Bhishma's capable hands.

When Vichitravirya came of age for marriage, Bhishma went to the swayamvara of the three daughters of the King of Kashi — Amba, Ambika, and Ambalika — and, single-handedly defeating every king present, carried off all three princesses. This was a duty performed for his brother's marriage, not for any desire of his own.

On the way, Amba revealed that she had already chosen King Shalva as her husband in her heart, and so Bhishma generously allowed her to go to him. But Shalva, fearing his own humiliation, rejected Amba, leaving her helpless and forced to return to Hastinapur — and after this rejection, her story turns toward a different, tragic direction that will unfold in the parvas ahead.

Ambika and Ambalika were duly married to Vichitravirya, but unfortunately, within a short time, Vichitravirya fell ill with consumption and died an untimely death without fathering any child, giving rise to a grave crisis of succession for the throne of Hastinapur.
chapters.moral: Even service rendered impartially out of duty to one's brother can, if circumstances turn adverse, unknowingly become the cause of deep suffering for someone else.

chapters.title: The Birth of Dhritarashtra, Pandu, and Vidura Through Niyoga
paragraphs: Satyavati, deeply anxious for the continuation of the lineage, asked Bhishma to break his vow and take the throne, but Bhishma, honoring his unbreakable vow, humbly refused — however dire the circumstances.

Satyavati then remembered her own son from before her marriage, Maharishi Vedavyasa, born to her by the sage Parashara. She asked Vyasa to father children with Vichitravirya's widows through the practice of niyoga, so that the lineage could continue — an accepted, dharma-sanctioned custom of that age.

Seeing Vyasa's fearsome, ascetic form, Ambika closed her eyes in fear, and as a result her son Dhritarashtra was born blind. Ambalika turned pale with fear, and so her son Pandu was born pale-complexioned and frail from birth.

Satyavati asked for the attempt to be made once more, but this time Ambika, in her place, sent her maidservant. This maid, without any fear or hesitation, came before Vyasa with perfect composure, and so her son Vidura was born exceptionally healthy, wise, and righteous — though, being the son of a maidservant, he was excluded from the succession to the throne.
chapters.moral: Fear and hesitation can shape a person's destiny from the very moment of birth, while calm, fearless acceptance becomes the greatest blessing of all.

chapters.title: The Marriages of Gandhari and Kunti — The Birth of the Hundred Kauravas
paragraphs: The blind Dhritarashtra was married to Gandhari, princess of Gandhara, who, upon learning immediately after the wedding that her husband was sightless, bound her own eyes with a cloth forever, resolving that she would never enjoy any comfort or ability beyond her husband's — a remarkable proof of her devotion.

Pandu was married to Kunti of the Yadava line and to Madri, princess of Madra. Kunti had received a divine mantra in her childhood from the sage Durvasa, by which she could invoke any deity and receive a child from him. She had tested the power of this mantra in her youth by invoking the Sun-god, secretly giving birth to a son named Karna, whom, fearing social disgrace, she set adrift on a river.

Gandhari, upon conceiving, suffered a long, unusual pregnancy that lasted two years. Finally, striking her own womb in frustration, she gave birth to a mass of flesh, which Maharishi Vyasa, through his yogic power, divided into a hundred parts and placed in vessels filled with ghee, from which a hundred sons and one daughter were born in turn.

The eldest of these hundred sons, Duryodhana, was born amid inauspicious omens — the howling of jackals, storms, and outbreaks of fire — seeing which the learned, including Vidura, warned everyone that this child would in the future become the cause of his own lineage's destruction, and advised that he be abandoned. But Dhritarashtra, blinded by paternal love, rejected this counsel.
chapters.moral: Ignoring ominous signs and deciding out of blind affection, however natural it may seem, can bring about ruinous consequences in the future.

chapters.title: Pandu's Curse and Retreat to the Forest
paragraphs: Pandu was a skilled archer and a valiant king, who in the early years of his reign conquered many kingdoms and expanded the borders of Hastinapur. One day, while hunting, he shot an arrow at a pair of deer — who were in truth a sage and his wife, engaged in intimacy in the form of deer.

The dying sage laid a terrible curse upon Pandu — that whenever he in future attempted to unite intimately with a woman, he would die at that very instant, just as Pandu had taken the sage's life at the very moment of his intimacy.

Deeply shaken by this dreadful curse, Pandu renounced the kingdom and all worldly pleasures and resolved to live an ascetic life in the forest along with his two queens, Kunti and Madri, entrusting the governance of Hastinapur to his blind brother Dhritarashtra.

In the forest, Pandu suffered for a long time from the deep anguish of childlessness, for the curse prevented him from becoming a father himself — and this very anxiety became the backdrop for Kunti's use of her divine mantra, which would give rise to the extraordinary birth of the Pandavas.
chapters.moral: A single unconsidered act can bring about long-lasting, irreversible consequences — yet divine grace can open new paths beyond any curse.

chapters.title: The Birth of the Pandavas
paragraphs: Pandu, distressed by his childlessness, asked Kunti to use her divine mantra once again, this time righteously, for the continuation of the lineage. Kunti first invoked Dharmaraja (Yama), from whom Yudhishthira was born, endowed from birth with an extraordinary devotion to truth and dharma.

She then invoked Vayu, the wind-god, from whom Bhima was born, blessed with astonishing physical strength and courage, and then invoked Indra, from whom Arjuna was born, who was destined to become renowned as the greatest archer in the world.

Madri, with Kunti's permission to use the same mantra once, invoked the Ashwini twins, from whom she received twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva, who became exceptionally skilled in horsemanship and astrology respectively.

Thus Pandu's five sons, though divinely conceived, were regarded in the eyes of the world as Pandu's own righteous sons, and became known as the "Pandavas" — each bearing the qualities of his divine father, together forming an extraordinary, well-balanced brotherhood.
chapters.moral: When human limits become obstacles, divine grace and righteous means can open the door to new possibilities — provided they are embraced with good intent.

chapters.title: The Deaths of Pandu and Madri, and Kunti's Return to Hastinapur
paragraphs: After years of ascetic life in the forest, one beautiful spring morning, Pandu, momentarily enchanted by Madri's extraordinary beauty and forgetting his curse, was drawn toward her — and suffered the immediate, dreadful consequence of that lapse, dying instantly.

Madri, blaming herself for her husband's death, sank into deep grief and remorse, and entrusting the care of her two sons, Nakula and Sahadeva, to Kunti, resolved to become sati and join her husband in death.

The sages of the hermitage, moved by this tragic event, safely escorted Kunti and the five Pandavas to Hastinapur, where they related to Bhishma, Vidura, and Dhritarashtra the full account of Pandu's death and the divine origin of the Pandavas.

The entire populace of Hastinapur gave the Pandavas a heartfelt welcome — though from this very moment, unknowingly, was also sown the seed of that long, ultimately ruinous rivalry between the Kauravas and Pandavas that would become the central story of the parvas to come.
chapters.moral: A single moment's forgetfulness cannot avert what destiny has written — yet true remorse and a sense of responsibility preserve dignity even in grief.

chapters.title: The Arrival of Guru Dronacharya and the Education of the Princes
paragraphs: From childhood, the Kauravas and Pandavas grew up together in Hastinapur, but Duryodhana's heart had already conceived a deep jealousy of Bhima's extraordinary physical strength — a jealousy that would give rise to many secret, wicked schemes in time to come.

During this period, Acharya Drona, a Brahmin exceptionally skilled in the art of weaponry, arrived at Hastinapur after being insulted by his childhood friend King Drupada, and, at Bhishma's request, agreed to teach the princes the art of arms.

Dronacharya gave all the princes thorough instruction in archery, mace-fighting, and other martial skills, but he recognized in Arjuna, in particular, an extraordinary focus, dedication, and talent, and declared him his most beloved, finest disciple.

Guru Drona promised Arjuna that he would make him the greatest archer in the world — a promise he fulfilled through Arjuna's remarkable dedication and discipline, though this very promise would also become the backdrop for the injustice done to another extraordinary disciple named Ekalavya.
chapters.moral: A promise a guru makes to his disciple, however noble, can sometimes also become the cause of injustice toward other deserving souls.

chapters.title: Ekalavya's Devotion to His Guru
paragraphs: Ekalavya, the son of a Nishada chieftain, came to Dronacharya with an intense desire to learn archery, but Drona, knowing him to be of low birth, and bound by his commitment to the princes, refused to accept him as a disciple.

Ekalavya, not the least deterred by this refusal, returned to the forest and there set up a clay image of Dronacharya, taking it alone as his guru, and practiced archery in solitude through tireless, disciplined self-study.

Some time later, when the princes, hunting in the forest, witnessed Ekalavya's extraordinary skill — he had silenced a barking dog's mouth with arrows purely by sound — they were stunned. Dronacharya was astonished to learn that Ekalavya had made himself even more skilled than Arjuna.

To honor the promise he had made to Arjuna, Drona asked Ekalavya for his right thumb as guru-dakshina. Ekalavya, without a moment's hesitation, cut off his thumb and offered it as proof of his devotion to his guru — though this forever weakened his archery. This story is regarded as one of the most supreme, yet most poignant, examples of selfless devotion to one's guru in all of Bhagavata literature.
chapters.moral: True devotion to a guru needs no formal acceptance — yet this story also reminds us that justice can sometimes be swayed by birth and circumstance.

chapters.title: Karna's Appearance at the Tournament of Arms
paragraphs: When their training was complete, Dronacharya arranged a grand tournament of arms to display the princes' skills, attended by all of Hastinapur, including the royal family. Arjuna enchanted the entire gathering with his extraordinary archery.
At that very moment, an unknown, radiant young man, Karna, entered the arena, and displaying skill equal to Arjuna's — indeed, even more extraordinary — openly challenged him to a duel.

When the question of Karna's lineage arose, and it was revealed that he was a suta's son (a charioteer's son), Kripacharya declared the duel improper, arguing that one of low birth could not stand against a prince, leaving Karna humiliated and standing in silence.

At this moment, Duryodhana, seeking an opportunity to humble Arjuna, immediately declared Karna the king of Anga, granting him royal status and thus making him eligible for the duel. Karna, deeply grateful for this unexpected generosity, bound himself in lifelong, unbreakable friendship and loyalty to Duryodhana — a friendship that would go on to determine the whole of his destiny.
chapters.moral: A generous, well-timed honor can bind a wounded heart in lifelong loyalty, whatever the motive behind it may have been.

chapters.title: Dronacharya's Guru-Dakshina — Victory Over Drupada
paragraphs: When their training was complete, Dronacharya asked the princes for a single guru-dakshina — that they capture King Drupada of Panchala and bring him before him, wishing to avenge the old insult inflicted by his childhood friend.

The Kauravas made the first attempt but were defeated by Drupada's army and returned. Then the Pandavas, led by Arjuna, attacked Drupada's army, and through Arjuna's extraordinary valor, Drupada was defeated and taken captive.

Dronacharya told Drupada that he still considered him his childhood friend, and, keeping only half the kingdom as his revenge, respectfully returned the other half to Drupada, declaring that now, being kings of equal standing, they could be friends once more.

Drupada, deeply wounded within by this humiliation, began to burn with an intense desire for revenge, and undertook a sacrifice to obtain a son capable of slaying Dronacharya — a sacrifice from which Dhrishtadyumna, and Draupadi herself, would in time miraculously appear.
chapters.moral: An insult, however many years later, can give rise to a fire of vengeance that becomes the foundation of vast events to come.

chapters.title: Jealousy Over the Crown Prince, and the Plot of the House of Lac
paragraphs: Yudhishthira, being the eldest and exceptionally righteous, was declared crown prince of Hastinapur, bringing joy to the people — but Duryodhana's heart burned with jealousy and insecurity, believing the throne to be rightfully his own.

Duryodhana, together with his uncle Shakuni and Karna, devised a wicked scheme to destroy the Pandavas forever. They persuaded Dhritarashtra to suggest that the Pandavas be sent for a time to the town of Varanavata, where a religious festival was being held.

Secretly, Duryodhana had a house built for the Pandavas' residence at Varanavata, made entirely of lac, ghee, and other highly flammable materials, planning that at the right moment this "House of Lac" would be set ablaze, burning the Pandavas and Kunti alive.

Vidura, who through his extraordinary wisdom and network of spies had become fully aware of this entire conspiracy, warned Yudhishthira in a secret coded language, without letting Dhritarashtra or Duryodhana suspect anything at all.
chapters.moral: Arrogance nurtured by blind affection does not hesitate even to plot the destruction of its own family — but a vigilant, wise friend can avert even the gravest danger in time.

chapters.title: The Pandavas' Escape from the House of Lac
paragraphs: Yudhishthira, understanding Vidura's secret signal, warned his brothers, and together they had a secret tunnel dug from the House of Lac leading out beyond the town — all accomplished with the utmost secrecy, without arousing anyone's suspicion.

When the conspirators set fire to the House of Lac on the appointed night, the Pandavas and Kunti escaped safely through the pre-dug tunnel. By coincidence, a Nishada woman with her five sons had taken shelter in that house that same night, and they were burned to death in the fire.

Seeing these six bodies, all of Hastinapur came to believe that Kunti and the five Pandavas had perished in the disaster. Duryodhana and Shakuni rejoiced inwardly, while Bhishma, Vidura, and the rest of the city sank into deep grief — though Vidura alone knew within that the Pandavas were safe.

The Pandavas, taking advantage of this moment, began wandering secretly through the forests, disguised as an ordinary Brahmin family, waiting for the right time to reveal their true identity once more.
chapters.moral: However secret and well-planned a conspiracy may be, it is those who prepare beforehand with vigilance and foresight who ultimately escape unharmed.

chapters.title: The Slaying of Hidimba and Bhima's Marriage to Hidimbi
paragraphs: Wandering through the forests disguised as Brahmins, the Pandavas one day arrived in the territory of a fearsome demon named Hidimba, who hunted and devoured human beings. Hidimba sent his sister Hidimbi to kill these newcomers.

Hidimbi, upon seeing Bhima's extraordinary, striking strength and beauty, fell instantly in love with him, and instead of obeying her brother's command, took the form of a beautiful woman and appeared before Bhima, expressing her love and her wish to marry him.

When Hidimba, enraged by his sister's delay, arrived himself, a fierce duel broke out between him and Bhima, in which Bhima, through his extraordinary strength, slew Hidimba. With Kunti and Yudhishthira's consent, Bhima married Hidimbi — though this marriage was bound by the condition that it would last only until she bore him a son.

From this marriage was born an extraordinary, mighty son named Ghatotkacha, who would in time prove to be an exceptionally important and valiant warrior for the Pandavas in the great war of Kurukshetra.
chapters.moral: Love can arise even in the most unexpected circumstances, and such bonds can later prove invaluable.

chapters.title: The Slaying of Bakasura
paragraphs: Continuing their wanderings, the Pandavas came to stay in a Brahmin's house in the town of Ekachakra. There they learned that this town lived in terror of a fearsome demon named Bakasura, who each week demanded an abundant meal along with the sacrifice of one human being from a different family.

One day, it was the turn of the very Brahmin family sheltering the Pandavas, and Kunti, seeing their pitiable plight, resolved to volunteer her son Bhima for this dreadful task, knowing Bhima possessed the extraordinary strength to face this demon.

Bhima took the cart of food meant for Bakasura into the forest himself and ate the entire meal along the way. When the enraged Bakasura arrived, a long, ferocious duel broke out between the two, in which Bhima finally broke the demon's back and slew him.

Thus the whole town was freed forever from this long-standing terror, though the Pandavas kept their true identity hidden — the feat became known only as the extraordinary valor of a Brahmin's son, who had ended the demon's reign of terror.
chapters.moral: True valor should be inspired not by the desire for fame, but by a sense of duty to protect the helpless.

chapters.title: Draupadi's Swayamvara
paragraphs: King Drupada arranged a grand swayamvara for the marriage of his extraordinary daughter Draupadi, who had emerged from a sacrificial fire. He set an exceedingly difficult contest of marksmanship — to string a bow and, looking only at the reflection below, pierce a rotating fish-shaped target mounted high above.

Hearing of this from Ekachakra, the Pandavas too arrived at the swayamvara, disguised as Brahmins. After many powerful kings, and Karna himself, failed at this difficult feat, it was announced in the assembly that any Brahmin present could also attempt the contest.

Arjuna, in his Brahmin disguise, stepped forward, and with extraordinary focus and skill, successfully pierced the difficult target, leaving the entire assembly stunned, and Draupadi placed the wedding garland around his neck.

Seeing this, many of the kings present, feeling especially humiliated that a Brahmin had defeated them all, rose in anger to attack, but Arjuna and Bhima together successfully repelled them, thereby securing Draupadi safely.
chapters.moral: True skill and focus are never beholden to outward appearance or social status — they reveal themselves in any circumstance.

chapters.title: The Marriage of Draupadi to All Five Pandavas
paragraphs: When Arjuna brought Draupadi to the potter's house where the Pandavas and Kunti were staying, Kunti, without looking, gave the customary instruction that whatever they had brought should be shared equally among themselves — not knowing that her sons had brought, this time, not alms, but Draupadi herself.

Regarding their mother's word as inviolable, and with Yudhishthira observing that this event seemed itself to be a part of divine will, the Pandavas arrived at the extraordinary, unprecedented decision that Draupadi would become the wife of all five brothers equally.

Vyasa himself came and clarified the propriety of this extraordinary marriage, revealing that Draupadi, in a previous life, had been an ascetic woman who had asked Lord Shiva five times for a husband, and so had received this extraordinary boon of five husbands.

Thus Draupadi was duly married to all five Pandavas. King Drupada and his son Dhrishtadyumna also accepted this extraordinary arrangement, and it was through this very swayamvara that the news reached Hastinapur that the Pandavas were alive, causing deep unease and anxiety among the Kauravas.
chapters.moral: Circumstances that seem unusual, if accepted with fidelity to truth and dharma, can prove to be part of a profound divine purpose.

chapters.title: The Founding of Indraprastha and the Burning of Khandavaprastha
paragraphs: On learning that the Pandavas were alive, on the advice of Bhishma and Vidura, Dhritarashtra decided to divide the kingdom — the Kauravas would keep Hastinapur, while the Pandavas were given a barren, forest-covered tract of land called Khandavaprastha, in what was, in truth, a shrewd and unequal division.

The Pandavas accepted this challenge without complaint, and with the help of Vishwakarma, the architect of the gods himself, established upon this barren land the magnificent, celestial city of Indraprastha, which soon became a symbol of prosperity, justice, and splendor.

During this time, Krishna and Arjuna together helped consign the Khandava forest to the fire-god Agni. This forest was protected by the gods, but Agni needed to consume it in order to regain his diminished strength; Arjuna and Krishna, with their divine weapons — the Gandiva bow and the Sudarshana Chakra — assisted Agni in this task.

Maya, an asura-architect who escaped this conflagration, out of gratitude built for the Pandavas the wondrous, magical Maya Sabha — a hall that would later become the setting for the ruinous game of dice. Thus the Adi Parva reaches its conclusion with the Pandavas firmly established at Indraprastha; in the Sabha Parva that follows awaits the story of Yudhishthira's Rajasuya sacrifice and the terrible game of dice that will lead the entire Bharata dynasty toward great destruction.
chapters.moral: Even an unequal, challenging beginning, if met with patience, effort, and divine help, can in time turn into extraordinary prosperity and glory.
